version.changelog: Security: replaced realistic-looking WIF example with obvious placeholder

llm.summary: The skill is mostly coherent with its stated purpose (an on-chain, client-side encrypted vault) but asks for a highly sensitive private key (CRITICAL_WIF), uses a development SDK version, and makes strong claims about the AI not being able to exfiltrate secrets that depend on how/where you run the CLI — these mismatches merit caution.

dimensions.detail: Name/description match the implementation: the CLI encrypts/decrypts credentials client-side and reads/writes ciphertext to Dash Platform. Requiring node, a Dash identity ID, and a private key (WIF) is consistent with the design (client-side encryption derived from your wallet key). The one mismatch is marketing language that implies the AI never has access to your key — in practice the CLI reads CRITICAL_WIF from the environment, so protection relies on runtime isolation, not an enforced technical barrier.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs the user to install the Evo SDK dev release, export CRITICAL_WIF and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID, run the provided Node CLI, and use a testnet faucet. The instructions do not ask the agent to read unrelated system files, but they do require placing a full private key in an environment variable and running code that will decrypt secrets into memory on the host — behaviour that is necessary for the stated purpose but expands the trust surface (process env, local cache, decrypted values in memory).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec is embedded in the registry (instruction-only install), but the SKILL.md requires installing a specific development release of @dashevo/evo-sdk. Using a dev-tag npm package is higher-risk than a stable release; there is no packaged binary or external URL download. The included code is a Node script that will run locally (no hidden network endpoints discovered in the code).
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The two required env vars (CRITICAL_WIF and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID) are directly relevant to the vault's cryptographic model. However, CRITICAL_WIF is a full private key (very high sensitivity). The SKILL.md repeatedly asserts the AI 'cannot exfiltrate' your key, but that assurance depends entirely on how the agent runtime isolates environment variables and on user behavior. The skill also derives a cache key from the private key and writes an encrypted cache to ~/.dashpass — both expected but increasing exposure if the host is compromised. This is proportionate to the declared functionality but carries substantial risk and should be treated as high-sensitivity access.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not always-enabled, does not request platform-wide persistence, and does not modify other skills. It creates a local cache under ~/.dashpass (user-level) which is expected for a vault. Autonomous invocation is allowed by default but not a unique privilege here; combining autonomous operation with access to CRITICAL_WIF raises operational risk but is not a mis-declaration by the skill itself.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill implements a plausible client-side encrypted vault, but it requires your full wallet private key (CRITICAL_WIF) in the environment — treat that as extremely sensitive. Before installing: (1) do NOT use a mainnet/private production WIF here; test with a throwaway testnet key first; (2) review the included Node script yourself or run it in an isolated environment (dedicated VM/container); (3) prefer DASHPASS_CACHE=none if you don't want a local encrypted cache; (4) be cautious when granting the agent runtime access to environment variables or allowing autonomous invocation — if the agent runtime can read env vars or run arbitrary code, it could obtain decrypted secrets; (5) consider pinning or auditing the @dashevo/evo-sdk version (dev tag is higher risk). If you can't verify runtime isolation and the code yourself, treat the request for CRITICAL_WIF as a blocker.
